691.quote_or_event: “A well-behaved monk should not sit on his hams, nor cross his arms, nor stretch out his legs, nor stand (too) close to his teacher.”
691.explanation: The discipline lecture sets out how a disciple keeps a respectful distance and posture before his teacher; a nearby verse (1.34) similarly has the monk stand 'neither too close by nor too far off' when receiving alms.
691.tie_back: The Kural pictures courtiers keeping a measured distance from the king, like people warming themselves at a fire; the Jain rule likewise asks for a measured, respectful distance before a superior.
691._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Shares the 'not too close' etiquette before a superior, but it lacks the Kural's fire image and its warning that a king's favour is dangerous.

692.quote_or_event: “Not resentful, having few wants, begging from strangers, and not being dainty, a wise man should not long for pleasant things, nor be sorry afterwards (for not having got them).”
692.explanation: In the trouble of 'respectful treatment', the monk is told to want little and not to long for pleasant things.
692.tie_back: The Kural advises the courtier not to covet what the king desires; the Jain verse teaches a more general freedom from craving pleasant things, which would keep one from coveting a ruler's enjoyments.
692._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Next-best only: Jain non-possessiveness (aparigraha) is general, and the Kural's point about not competing with the king, and being rewarded by him, has no counterpart.

693.quote_or_event: “A weak point in one's lord, even though small, must be guarded against. By means of a hole even small, water destroys a dam.”
693.explanation: Suvega warns Bahubali that failing to wait on his elder brother leaves room for informers to poison the king's mind, and that even a small breach in the lord's trust must be guarded against.
693.tie_back: The Kural warns that once a king grows suspicious no one can calm him; the Jain narrative likewise says even a small fault in the ruler's eyes must be guarded against before it bursts the dam.
693.source: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra 1.5, Part 1, 'Negotiations with Bahubali' (Hemachandra, tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS 1931)
693._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Close on guarding against a ruler's suspicion; it is a character's argument in the story (Bahubali rejects it), not doctrinal teaching.

694.quote_or_event: “One should always be meek, and not be talkative in the presence of the wise; one should acquire valuable knowledge, and avoid what is worthless.”
694.explanation: The sutra asks for meek, restrained behaviour and little talk in the presence of superiors; Uttaradhyayana 11.4 also lists 'not to be fond of mirth' as part of discipline.
694.tie_back: The Kural forbids whispering and shared laughter in the presence of the great; the Jain rule asks for quiet, restrained conduct before one's superiors.
694._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Same spirit of decorum before superiors, but it does not name whispering or exchanged smiles, so scored below 60.

695.quote_or_event: “…if he is always humble, steady, free from deceit and curiosity; if he abuses nobody…”
695.explanation: Among the fifteen marks of a well-behaved monk the sutra lists being free from curiosity, alongside humility and steadiness.
695.tie_back: The Kural forbids prying into the king's private talk or pressing him with questions; the Jain list counts freedom from curiosity as a mark of good discipline.
695._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (excerpt from a longer list, marked with ellipses). 'Free from curiosity' matches the restraint, but there is no reference to a ruler's secrets.

696.quote_or_event: “Guessing the teacher's thoughts and the purport of his words, one should express one's assent, and execute (what he desires to be done).”
696.explanation: The disciple is to read the teacher's unspoken intention and respond to it fittingly.
696.tie_back: The Kural asks the courtier to read the king's mood and choose the moment before speaking; the Jain rule likewise asks the disciple to read a superior's mind and respond in a way that fits it.
696._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong match on reading a superior's inner disposition; the Kural's emphasis on timing and agreeable words is only partly covered.

697.quote_or_event: “He should not tell anything sinful or meaningless or hurtful, neither for his own sake nor for anybody else's, nor without such a motive.”
697.explanation: The sutra forbids sinful, idle or harmful speech whatever the reason, whether for oneself or for another.
697.tie_back: The Kural says never to speak of useless or harmful things even if the king asks; the Jain rule bars meaningless or hurtful speech even when it is for someone else's sake.
697._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Close match on refusing fruitless or harmful talk even for another's sake; the Kural's positive half, telling the king what is truly worth wanting, is less explicit.

698.quote_or_event: “If you, fearless at the thought, ‘He is my brother,’ do not come, that is not fitting. Kings, whose essence is command, are not restrained by relationship.”
698.explanation: Suvega tells Bahubali that kinship with the Chakravartin is no excuse for failing to honour him as king, because royal authority is not set aside by family ties.
698.tie_back: The Kural forbids looking down on the king as 'my relative' or 'younger than me'; Suvega's speech makes the same point that kinship does not cancel the respect owed to the throne.
698.source: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra 1.5, Part 1, 'Negotiations with Bahubali' (Hemachandra, tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS 1931)
698._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Near-direct parallel on kinship versus royal dignity; it is the envoy's argument, which Bahubali rejects, and Jain tradition finally values Bahubali's renunciation over Bharata's claim.

699.quote_or_event: “He should never do anything disagreeable to the wise, neither in words nor deeds, neither openly nor secretly.”
699.explanation: The sutra says the disciple must never do what displeases his superiors, in word or deed, openly or in secret.
699.tie_back: The Kural warns those who think 'the king favours us' against doing what he would not accept; the Jain rule simply allows no exception, so favour gives no licence for conduct the superior would disapprove.
699._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Matches the core prohibition; the Kural's specific warning against presuming on favour is not stated.

700.quote_or_event: Gosala travelled with Mahavira for six years as a self-declared pupil. He later broke away, proclaimed himself a Tirthankara, and picked a quarrel with his former teacher. He hurled his magic fire (tejolesya) at Mahavira, but it turned back on him, and he died after repenting.
700.explanation: In Jain tradition Gosala's long familiarity with Mahavira did not breed reverence. It led to arrogance and open defiance, and that defiance brought about his own ruin.
700.tie_back: The Kural warns that the intimacy of 'we are old friends of the king' leads people into improper conduct and destroys them; Gosala's story shows an old companion presuming on the past, with the same result.
700.source: Bhagavati Sutra (Vyakhyaprajnapti), Shataka 15, as summarised by T.U. Mehta, The Path of Arhat, 'Association with Gosala' (jainworld.com)
700._accuracy_note: Paraphrase checked against T.U. Mehta's summary on jainworld.com. Scholars (e.g. Basham) regard the Jain account of Gosala as coloured by sectarian rivalry, and the setting is teacher and disciple, not king and courtier.
